strengths: Addresses a timely and relevant problem: reducing critic overhead and stabilizing end-to-end reinforcement learning for LLM-based multi-agent systems.

The proposed MHGPO framework is reasonably complete, combining group-relative advantage estimation, backward reward propagation, and three distinct rollout strategies with clear pseudocode and illustrative diagrams.

The empirical study goes beyond final accuracy by reporting training convergence, GPU memory, runtime, agent-level output changes, format penalties, intra-group similarity, and a qualitative case study.
Under the tested three-agent search setting, Fork-on-first and Round-robin appear to outperform or match MAPPO on most metrics while removing the large critic model.
The appendix provides the agent prompts, main hyperparameters, dataset choices, and implementation details, which partially supports reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central claim is overstated. MHGPO does not consistently outperform MAPPO across all variants and metrics: Independent Sampling is generally worse, FoF is slightly lower on 2Wiki EM, and RR is lower on MuSiQue accuracy.

Experimental scope is narrow for a method claimed to apply generally to MASs. Evidence is limited to one linear three-agent search architecture, one training dataset, one 8B instruction-tuned backbone, one epoch, and one group size.
Statistical rigor is insufficient: there are no multiple seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests, so gains of roughly 1–3 points cannot be clearly distinguished from run-to-run variance.

The baseline comparison is limited. Besides MAPPO, there is no comparison with direct multi-agent GRPO, independent PPO/GRPO per agent, HAPPO/CTDE methods, or an SFT-warm-up variant. The much larger Qwen2.5-72B system is evaluated only without MARL.

The heterogeneous-group advantage estimator lacks justification when outputs correspond to different intermediate prompts. In particular, Algorithm 5 appears to regroup singleton outputs from different original questions, which violates the same-prompt assumption underlying GRPO and may introduce prompt-difficulty bias; no importance correction or ablation is provided.

Credit assignment is still coarse: final F1 is propagated by simple averaging and supplemented with heuristic format penalties. The paper does not isolate the contributions of reward propagation, group normalization, and reward shaping.
Key ablations are missing, including group size G, Round-robin probabilities p_i, aggregation operators, reward propagation choices, critic size, and rollout/token budgets.

The efficiency analysis is restricted to averages over the first 50 training steps and does not report end-to-end wall-clock time, total generated tokens, or compute required to reach a target performance. A smaller critic could also narrow the memory gap with MAPPO.
Using the first 500 examples of the HotpotQA test set as a validation curve is methodologically questionable, especially if it informed design decisions; a separate development set should be used.

Reproducibility would be improved by releasing code and trained configurations, specifying random seeds, defining the Accuracy metric, detailing Wikipedia/index preprocessing, and clarifying the two listed learning rates.
The claim of training without warm-up is only weakly supported because the backbone is already instruction-tuned and no experiment compares against an SFT-warm-start condition.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and relevant problem: reducing the memory and instability of critic-based MARL for LLM-based multi-agent systems.

The proposed MHGPO framework is conceptually coherent: it combines parameter sharing, trajectory-level group sampling, backward propagation of final rewards, and critic-free relative advantage estimation.
The three rollout strategies—Independent Sampling, Fork-on-first, and Round-robin—provide an intuitive trade-off between computational cost and the ability to form heterogeneous comparison groups.
The empirical study includes three multi-hop QA datasets, efficiency measurements, and useful analyses of agent behavior, format penalties, intra-group similarity, and a qualitative case study.
The appendix supplies pseudocode, agent prompts, and some hyperparameters, which helps readers understand the implemented system.
weaknesses: The central claims are overstated. MHGPO does not consistently outperform MAPPO across all variants and metrics: IS is worse on HotpotQA, and RR is worse than MAPPO on MuSiQue accuracy. The conclusions should refer specifically to the best-performing FoF/RR configurations.

The method lacks a rigorous policy-gradient derivation. Backward reward propagation is defined as simple averaging over downstream agents, but no justification is given for this credit assignment, especially under branching trajectories, varying trajectory lengths, or stochastic upstream and downstream actions.

The sequence-level and token-level advantages are not clearly connected. Equation (5) defines an output-level advantage, while Equation (6) uses token-wise advantages, and the terminal-only reward assignment makes it unclear whether the scalar advantage is broadcast over all tokens or recomputed at each time step. Masks, zero-variance groups, and variable group sizes are also unaddressed.
Equation (4) is internally ambiguous: the text describes aggregation over direct successors, whereas the formula indexes all later agents j>k.

Round-robin regrouping is potentially problematic. Singleton outputs from different questions are shuffled and placed into the same comparison group, but GRPO-style relative advantages are normally computed among responses to the same prompt. Comparing F1-derived rewards across different questions can confound agent quality with question difficulty, and no ablation validates this design.

The evaluation protocol appears to use the first 500 samples from the test set as a validation set. This constitutes test-set leakage or, at minimum, requires a clean development split and re-evaluation without test-based monitoring.

Statistical evidence is weak: only one training run is reported, with no standard deviations, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Several out-of-domain gains over MAPPO are only around 1–3 points and may not be robust.

The evidence for generality is limited. All experiments use one fixed linear three-agent search pipeline, one shared 8B Llama backbone, and training on HotpotQA only. This does not substantiate claims about optimizing all MASs or non-shared, non-sequential agent architectures.

Important baselines and ablations are missing. There is no clear comparison with vanilla GRPO on complete trajectories, final-reward-only optimization, MHGPO without backward propagation, homogeneous-only grouping, or optimization without agent-specific penalties. MAPPO is also the only strong MARL baseline, and the alternating use of PPO in figures and MAPPO in the table is confusing.

The efficiency comparison is not fully controlled. MHGPO generates multiple group rollouts, but wall-clock and memory results are not normalized by the number of generated trajectories or tokens. The measurements are also restricted to the first 50 training steps.

Reproducibility is incomplete. No code release is stated, and the paper omits or does not clearly specify random seeds, decoding parameters, maximum output lengths, retrieval top-k and index construction, the chosen learning rate, reward normalization, evaluation scripts, and MAPPO hyperparameter tuning.

The novelty is somewhat incremental: the core approach largely adapts GRPO to multi-agent trajectories and adds straightforward rollout forking and reward averaging. The paper would benefit from a clearer distinction from ordinary GRPO applied to a flattened multi-agent trajectory.

The writing contains terminology and presentation issues, including interchangeable use of MAS and MASS, inconsistent PPO/MAPPO naming, typographical errors, and insufficient explanation of the Accuracy, EM, and F1 implementations. The anomalous 0.5 EM score for Single LLM+RL also needs explanation.

Overall, the idea is promising, but the current version is not yet sufficiently sound or reproducible for Findings. It requires corrected splits, repeated runs, controlled ablations, clearer formalization, and stronger baselines before publication.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and important NLP problem: end-to-end reinforcement learning for LLM-based multi-agent systems while avoiding the instability and computational cost of separately trained critic networks.

The proposed MHGPO framework is coherent and practically motivated, combining heterogeneous group-relative advantages, backward reward propagation, parameter sharing, and three rollout strategies with different efficiency/effectiveness trade-offs.

Fork-on-first and Round-robin are useful contributions: they reduce the rollout redundancy of Independent Sampling while still allowing downstream agents to receive relative learning signals across trajectories.

The empirical study shows consistent improvements over MAPPO on HotpotQA, 2WikiMultihopQA, and MuSiQue after training only on HotpotQA, including gains in Accuracy, Exact Match, and F1 without an SFT warm-up stage.

The paper provides useful supplementary evidence through convergence curves, GPU-memory and timing comparisons, agent-specific penalty curves, intra-group similarity analysis, output-pattern analysis, and a qualitative case study.
Reproducibility is reasonably supported by detailed pseudocode, agent prompts, hyperparameters, dataset descriptions, retrieval setup, and implementation details in the appendix.
weaknesses: The central heterogeneous-group advantage lacks theoretical justification. Unlike GRPO, which compares responses to the same prompt, FoF/RR can compare actions conditioned on different upstream outputs and therefore different agent states; cross-state reward normalization may introduce bias, but no bias-variance analysis is provided.

Several formal details are underspecified, especially how rewards are aggregated over branching successor trajectories and whether the scalar sequence-level advantage is broadcast across all tokens. The notation suggesting rewards only at the final token is potentially inconsistent with standard GRPO-style token-level optimization.

The causal evidence for why MHGPO works is limited. There are no controlled ablations of backward reward propagation, agent-specific penalties, heterogeneous grouping, group size G, or the Round-robin probabilities; the behavioral and similarity analyses are largely descriptive.

Experimental robustness is limited by a single random seed, absence of confidence intervals or significance tests, and relatively small differences among some MHGPO variants. The evaluation also uses one training dataset, one epoch, one 8B-parameter backbone, and one three-agent search architecture.
Although the method is claimed to apply to general MAS, validation is restricted to the MASS prototype. Qwen appears only as an unoptimized baseline, so cross-backbone generality is not established.

The baseline comparison is dominated by MAPPO. Independent Sampling is a useful internal ablation, but the paper would benefit from clearer comparison with a standard GRPO implementation and other recent LLM multi-agent RL or critic-free methods.

Efficiency results are averaged over only the first 50 training steps on one hardware/implementation configuration, and the critic is given the same large backbone as the actor. End-to-end cost per environment interaction and variance across runs are not reported.

Some reproducibility details remain unspecified, including an explicit code-release statement, exact answer-normalization rules for the reported Accuracy metric, and a few sampling and retrieval configuration details.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and important problem: end-to-end RL for LLM-based multi-agent search systems without the instability and memory overhead of a separate critic.

MHGPO is clearly formalized through backward reward propagation, heterogeneous-group advantage estimation, parameter sharing, and a GRPO-style objective. The three rollout strategies provide a useful efficiency–effectiveness trade-off.
The empirical results are strong on HotpotQA and show competitive average out-of-domain transfer to 2WikiMultihopQA and MuSiQue, while also reducing GPU memory and training time relative to MAPPO.

The evaluation includes several informative ablations: role-wise training, reward aggregation operators, final-reward-only training, group size, and training dynamics. These ablations directly support the claimed importance of joint multi-agent optimization and heterogeneous grouping.
The paper is generally well organized, with helpful diagrams, pseudocode, agent prompts, hyperparameters, and a theoretical appendix connecting the multi-agent formulation to single-context GRPO.
weaknesses: The empirical scope is narrower than the paper's broad framing. All RL training is on HotpotQA using one fixed linear three-agent pipeline, one static retrieval setup, one training epoch, and 8B-scale backbones. Generalization to branching or graph-like agent topologies, dynamic tools, larger models, and non-QA agentic tasks remains unsupported.

The main results in Table 1 do not report standard deviations, significance tests, or the number of seeds, even though several appendix tables do. This makes the smaller differences between MHGPO variants and strong baselines difficult to assess.

The claim of consistently outperforming strong baselines is too strong. On MuSiQue, MAPPO obtains higher F1 than the reported MHGPO variants, although MHGPO is competitive on EM/Accuracy and better on average out-of-domain performance.

The Round-robin grouping procedure is under-specified and potentially problematic. Algorithm 3 appears to regroup singleton rollouts across different root questions and possibly different agent stages without ensuring matched prompts. If this is cross-prompt normalization, it is not ordinary homogeneous GRPO grouping and can confound prompt difficulty; the paper should clarify the grouping keys and ablate this design.

The technical novelty is somewhat incremental: the method combines known ideas from parameter-shared MARL, reward broadcasting, and GRPO. The theoretical equivalence relies on the strong context-sufficiency assumption A3, and no approximation bounds, variance analysis, or stability guarantees are provided when that assumption fails.

Some reproducibility details remain incomplete, including an explicit code release, the exact answerer length-penalty threshold/formula, full optimizer and scheduling details, and whether the principal Table 1 results are single- or multi-seed runs.

Baseline coverage would be stronger with additional multi-agent RL methods such as HAPPO and with MHGPO applied to a second backbone model; the 72B Qwen results are only unoptimized references and do not establish scaling behavior.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and important problem: end-to-end reinforcement learning for LLM-based multi-agent retrieval systems without the memory and instability costs of a separate critic.

The main recipe is intuitive and practically appealing: parameter sharing, backward propagation of terminal rewards, per-agent GRPO-style normalization, and heterogeneous comparison of rollouts branching from the same user question.

The appendix makes a serious formal effort to connect MHGPO to single-context GRPO through token-level equivalence results under explicitly stated assumptions. This is more rigorous than many applied LLM-RL papers.

The empirical study is reasonably broad for a first study: three multi-hop QA datasets, several strong single-agent RAG and MARL baselines, training-dynamics plots, resource measurements, reward and role ablations, group-size analysis, and a qualitative case study.

The FoF and RR strategies expose a useful performance–efficiency trade-off. In particular, FoF(os) obtains the strongest reported results, while RR reduces GPU memory and step time relative to MAPPO and FoF.
weaknesses: The technical contribution is somewhat incremental. Parameter sharing, global-reward broadcasting, and group-relative advantages are already standard in MARL and GRPO; the principal novelty is applying normalization across rollouts with different local agent prompts. The paper does not fully establish when this heterogeneous normalization is preferable to a state-conditioned or leave-one-out baseline beyond empirical intuition.

The Round-robin construction is conceptually ambiguous. For agents before a late fork point, the paper describes grouping one rollout with other batch samples that fork at the same agent, but those samples generally have different root questions and local prompts. They are therefore not 'homogeneous groups' under the paper's earlier same-input definition, and normalizing rewards across different questions can confound action quality with question difficulty. The group-identifier scope in Algorithms 3 and 5 is also not fully unambiguous.

The theoretical results depend on strong assumptions, especially deterministic prompt construction and context sufficiency (A2–A3). Real search agents often receive compressed or incomplete upstream context, exactly the regime in which the proposed heterogeneous groups are claimed to help. The proofs therefore establish an idealized correspondence to GRPO, but not variance reduction, stability, or improved credit assignment when those assumptions fail.

Experimental scope is narrower than the paper's general framing. All learned experiments use one fixed linear three-agent Rewriter–Reranker–Answerer pipeline, static Wikipedia retrieval with Contriever, one 8B Llama backbone, and one epoch of HotpotQA training. The OOD datasets remain similar Wikipedia-style multi-hop QA tasks; there is no evaluation on open-ended search, tool-use planning, larger models, nonlinear agent topologies, or varying numbers of agents.

Statistical rigor is incomplete. The main results in Table 1 do not report standard deviations, numbers of seeds, or significance tests, even though some gains over MAPPO and R1-Searcher are modest and MAPPO is shown to be unstable. Efficiency results are implementation-sensitive and averaged only over the first 50 steps, and details such as retrieval budget, document aggregation, and baseline tuning are not fully comparable.

Reproducibility could be substantially improved. The manuscript provides prompts and some hyperparameters, but no explicit code/artifact pointer is visible, and several details are missing: PPO epochs, optimizer settings, maximum lengths, retrieval top-K, document deduplication/aggregation, exact format-reward formulas and thresholds, and the evaluation normalization implementation.

The composite format rewards explain a large portion of the gains. Table 4 shows sharp degradation when agent-specific penalties are removed, especially for MAPPO. Although MHGPO remains better with terminal reward only, the experiments do not completely isolate heterogeneous grouping from reward shaping and other implementation choices.

Some claims are overstated. MHGPO-IS does not outperform MAPPO on HotpotQA or either OOD dataset, so statements that the MHGPO family 'consistently' outperforms strong baselines should be qualified to refer specifically to FoF/RR variants. Similarly, broad claims about general multi-agent search systems are supported only by a narrow QA pipeline.

Overall, the core FoF method is promising and the paper is close to Findings quality, but the unclear RR grouping, limited evaluation regime, absent main-table uncertainty estimates, and reproducibility gaps prevent a clear positive recommendation in its current form.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: end-to-end reinforcement learning for LLM-based multi-agent search systems without relying on extensive prompt engineering, per-agent supervised fine-tuning, or a costly separate critic.

MHGPO is technically coherent. Backward reward propagation captures indirect upstream–downstream dependencies, while heterogeneous-group advantage estimation compares rollouts sharing a root task but differing in intermediate decisions, explicitly targeting global rather than purely local agent performance.

The IS, FoF, RR, and FoF(os) sampling strategies provide useful and practically relevant performance–compute trade-offs. RR is particularly compelling because it retains strong task performance while substantially reducing memory and training time.

The theoretical appendix adds rigor by establishing distributional and token-level learning-signal equivalence between the MAS view and a constructed single-context transcript under clearly stated assumptions. The authors are transparent that the context-sufficiency assumption is idealized.

The empirical study is broad within the search-QA setting: it uses three multi-hop QA datasets, multiple answer metrics, strong RL and RAG baselines, training curves, resource measurements, and ablations of role training, reward aggregation, terminal rewards, and group size.

The reported gains are substantial on HotpotQA and remain visible out of domain; for example, MHGPO-FoF(os) reaches 50.858 F1 on HotpotQA, compared with 46.400 for MAPPO and 45.392 for R1-Searcher(GRPO).
weaknesses: Generalizability is limited. All experiments use one linear three-agent QA pipeline, a static Wikipedia corpus and contriever, English multi-hop questions, a single shared 8B backbone, and one training epoch. Broader claims about general MASs would require open-ended search, dynamic tools, branching or graph-like interactions, non-shared policies, and larger models.

Statistical evidence is incomplete. The main table does not report standard deviations or significance tests for MAPPO and other key baselines, and some out-of-domain differences—especially for RR—are small enough that seed variance could affect the conclusions.

Heterogeneous grouping can confound local and upstream credit assignment for downstream agents because their actions are conditioned on different upstream outputs. RR mitigates this by mixing homogeneous and heterogeneous comparisons, but there is no variance or bias analysis for the realistic setting where the context-sufficiency assumption fails.

The efficiency evidence is not fully normalized. Figure 6 reports GPU-memory percentage and average per-step time, but not generated-token counts, tool-call counts, or complete end-to-end wall-clock cost. FoF and FoF(os) are slower than MAPPO, so the strongest efficiency claim is primarily supported by RR.

Reproducibility would be improved by a code release and more precise specification of the agent-specific reward coefficients, length thresholds, and group-identifier construction. The relationship between the group identifier in Equation 5 and its assignment in Algorithm 5 is somewhat ambiguous.

The formal equivalence depends on the strong A3 context-sufficiency assumption. It provides a useful conceptual bridge to GRPO but does not by itself establish convergence or stability for practical multi-context systems with incomplete local contexts.
